title: The Great Fire of London
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: In the early hours of Sunday 2 September 1666, a fire broke out in a bakery in Pudding Lane, in the City of London. The baker, Thomas Farriner, and his family escaped through an upstairs window, but sparks from the oven had already set light to a pile of firewood. At first nobody thought the fire was serious. Fires were common in the crowded city, and most were put out within hours. This one, however, was to burn for four days and become the greatest disaster in the history of the city.

Several things allowed the fire to spread so quickly. The houses in the old city were built of wood and covered with tar, and their upper floors leaned so close across the narrow streets that neighbours could almost shake hands from their windows. It had also been a hot, dry summer, and a strong wind from the east carried burning pieces of wood from roof to roof. The warehouses beside the river were full of oil, tallow and coal, which fed the flames and produced a heat that could be felt a mile away.

The authorities were slow to act. The usual way of stopping a fire was to pull down the houses in its path, to create a gap that the flames could not cross, but the Lord Mayor hesitated to give the order, since the owners would have to be paid. By the time King Charles II took charge, much of the city was already burning. The king and his brother, the Duke of York, worked beside ordinary people, passing buckets of water and giving out money to the men who fought the flames.

The most famous account of the fire was written by Samuel Pepys, a government official, in his diary. He watched from a boat on the river and described the sky as red as a furnace. He also acted to protect his possessions: he buried his wine and a valuable Parmesan cheese in a pit in his garden. His diary is valuable to historians because it records what an ordinary person saw and felt, not only what the kings and ministers did, and it gives a vivid picture of the fear in the crowded streets.

By Wednesday, the wind had dropped, and the fire was brought under control, helped by the blowing up of houses with gunpowder to make wide gaps. When it was over, about thirteen thousand houses and eighty-seven churches had been destroyed, including the old St Paul's Cathedral. Roughly seventy thousand of the city's eighty thousand inhabitants had lost their homes. Remarkably, only a handful of deaths were officially recorded, although historians suspect that the poor, whose deaths were not noted, may have died in larger numbers.

The rebuilding of London took more than ten years. Plans for a completely new city with wide straight streets were drawn up by the architect Christopher Wren, but they were abandoned because landowners wished to rebuild on their old plots. New laws, however, required that houses be made of brick or stone, and that streets be made wider. Wren designed fifty-one new churches and a new St Paul's, whose great dome is still the most familiar part of the London skyline.

The fire also left a lasting mark on the way people think about safety. The first fire insurance companies were founded soon afterwards, and they employed their own fire fighters, who would only help buildings that carried the company's badge. A tall column, the Monument, was built near Pudding Lane in the 1670s to remember the disaster. It is 202 feet high, which is exactly the distance from its base to the place where the bakery once stood, and visitors can still climb its 311 steps.
